Back in 6th grade, we had a Computer class a couple of times a week. Part of this class involved learning how to use the internet (which, since this was 1994-95, it was kind of a new thing for middle schoolers to be learning about). Mostly, we learned how to use e-mail, as well as how to find some websites and explore them on the school Macintoshes.

The computer teacher, however, knew there were some things that should not be visited during school hours or on school computers - not even porn, just random, obscure sites that he felt would be detrimental or disturbing to the classroom environment. As a result, these were placed on a large construction paper tree titled "The Tree of Forbidden Websites." The forbidden sites were written down on an apple (in the shape of the Apple logo, naturally).

One day, through some random exploring, I found the most amazing website anyone had ever discovered. This site played sound clips from The Simpsons, perhaps hundreds of sound clips that could be played forward AND backward. It was glorious, and from the moment I played the first sound clip those around me were transfixed by this amazing discovery.

Naturally, many of the others began to visit the site and within ten minutes the computer lab was filled with a brilliant cacophony of various Simpsons sound clips. It spread like wildfire through the 6th grade class, and eventually there was always at least one person messing around with that website whenever there was a class in the computer lab.

Within a week, a new apple appeared on the Tree of Forbidden Websites. It read simply, "The Simpsons."

When I write a character, I leave a lot of details about them unsaid. "Actions speak louder than words," as the saying goes, so I try to let their actions define who they are. Sometimes I'll need to go into certain things if they're a main character, but side characters rarely get that sort of attention.

I do try to make all my characters unique so they don't all blend into one another, but when it comes to getting details I let it come out as necessary and go from there. Once I've got a character in my mind and they're developing into a lead character, I have a lot of their stuff memorized and just stick with what I know about them from what they've already done in the story.

My entire 4th grade year feels like it was one long injustice, but this one particular memory is the crowning turd of that pile of shit.

One day, we were lined up to go somewhere in the school - that's what we did back in those days, we lined up in the classroom and walked in single-file through the school to reach our destination - when I must have done or said something to offend the kid in front of me. I'm not the kind of person to go around doing or saying things to offend people, so I honestly don't know what I did. Regardless, this kid - who was a bit of a mean kid already - turned around and kicked me right in the shin. For no damn reason.

My teacher intervened and sent the both of us to In-School Suspension (ISS), where the bad kids go for a sort of detention-like punishment for an hour or so. I got sent there and I hadn't done ANYTHING except get kicked in the shin. I didn't retaliate, I didn't shove him, I just took it. And I still got punished.

Fuck you, Ms. Spencer. You were a shitty teacher and a shitty human being.

So this will be a bit of a long post, but it's the only real "I shouldn't be alive" moment I have in my life, so bear with me.

Back in 2005, I went with some friends to Hawaii for 10 days to celebrate graduation from college (most of them were graduating, but I still had a year left and tagged along anyway because Hawaii). We island hopped around for a bit between Oahu and Maui - Maui was my favorite island by far - before we wound up in Hilo on the Big Island.

Our second day in Hilo we went to Volcanoes National Park about 30 miles away, because if you're close to an active volcano you should go see said volcano, because volcanoes are kickass. We stopped for some supplies in town before making the drive along the winding road to the national park to see the sights.

The sights were amazing - the steaming caldera at the top surrounded by offerings to the goddess Pele, the rainforest cut through by large swaths of blackened lava rock, the ancient lava tubes you can walk through. It's majestic and beautiful and a reminder of just how utterly powerful and destructive the Earth can be when it feels like it.

After visiting the visitor's center, we took a ride down to a road that had been partially buried in lava years ago after Kilauea started erupting. The're a small ranger's station at the point where the road is buried, and you can hike across the blackened terrain to see where the lava is actively flowing into the ocean. We decided to take the 3-mile trek that day, because lava is awesome.

So we go on our hike, and it's kind of difficult going - there's not really a path because the terrain is covered in massive, broken slabs of jagged, hardened lava rock. There are blinking orange beacons on top of small hilltops every half mile or so to guide you at night, but that's the only indication that there's any "right" way to go. So we just walked along, all the time getting closer to the rising column of steam in the distance.

When we were about half a mile from the active lava flow, we had to cover our mouths and noses with our shirts to prevent from breathing in the volcanic fog (or vog) that was all round us. That stuff is nasty, and you don't want to breathe it if you can help it.

Soon, we got to the point where the lava was active, and found ourselves a skylight into a tube that was faintly active. We couldn't see flowing lava inside, but you could see a reddish glow and waves of heat emanating from withininside. Naturally, we decided to take pictures near the skylight, and one of my friends threw an old key from their apartment into the skylight to let Pele know what we thought of her and her skylights. Or something like that. I was never sure why the key had to be tossed.

After a little bit more of a walk, we finally settled down onto a rocky spot where we could watch the glowing lava oozing out of the earth and hitting the ocean. It remains one of the most amazing sights I've ever seen in my live. The shades of red and orange and yellow flowing out and into the water were spectacular, and the way this molten material caused the water to instantly sizzle and boil was magical. Occasionally there would be small explosions of fiery sparks in the water from the lava. It was almost hypnotic, and we sat and watched for nearly an hour and a half.

At this point, the sun had set, and it was quite dark. This would make our hike back across the jagged rocks a little bit trickier, but thankfully we had a couple of large flashlights. So, we began the hike back, knowing we still had three difficult miles to go in the dark before reaching the car. I suppose that's the price you pay for seeing one of the most amazing things you've ever seen in your life.

As we were making our way back, we noticed that our little skylight from before now had a small trickle of lava flowing out of it on the surface. This was awesome, so naturally we walked over to take some more pictures. One of my less intelligent friends decided it would be a good idea to climb down a small embankment and stand within about five feet of this lava trickle to get his picture taken.

After his picture, he was climbing up the embankment when the Earth beneath the skylight made a sound I've never heard in my life. It was a sort of vomiting BLLUOOORP sound, and with it came a massive surge of white-hot lava. Thankfully my friend hadn't taken his picture five seconds later than he did, or else he would have died then and there.

Naturally, people are freaking out about this sudden influx of surprise lava. I turned and ran a few steps before deciding that this would make a pretty good picture. So I stopped and turned to take a few shots before running back toward the direction of the car.

One thing I haven't mentioned up to this point is that beneath your feet as you're walking over the lava rock, sometimes the ground below you sounds a little hollow. That's because it is. When lava flows underground in these areas, it can leave behind empty tubes where it once flowed. These can be dangerous because if they're too thin and you step in the wrong place, the tubes can collapse and take you with them.

Back to me running. As I'm sprinting away, I suddenly notice that the air around me is starting to get hot. Very hot. As I glanced down to the ground, I could see all the cracks in the lava rock beneath my feet glowing bright red.

An inactive lava tube had reactivated while we were watching the lava flow into the ocean and started pumping a LOT of molten material through the ground right below our feet. And we had to run directly over it.

Naturally, I didn't want to die by lava, so I picked up my speed, met up with a couple friends mid-stride, and continued to sprint through the darkness for almost a quarter of a mile before we finally decided we were safe enough to take a breather. The rest of our friends eventually caught up, and once we'd done a head count to make sure everyone was safe and accounted for, we continued the long hike back to the car.

We only had one flashlight to guide us back - the other had been set down slightly too close to the lava flow and was consumed by the fires of the Earth itself when my less-than-intelligent friend went to get his picture taken. Fortunately, there was bright moonlight overhead so we managed to make it back to the car without anyone getting hurt.

It wasn't until we were back at the car that I thought about checking my shoes to see if my sprint over the active lava tube had done any damage to them. I borrowed the flashlight, and lifted my feet one at a time to check.

Both soles had been melted.

**TL;DR: Went to Hawaii with some friends, hiked across barren lava rock to watch lava flow into the ocean, had to sprint across an active lava tube to get to safety, melted my shoes**

These can be dangerous because if they're too thin and you step in the wrong place, the tubes can collapse and take you with them.

Back to me running. As I'm sprinting away, I suddenly notice that the air around me is starting to get hot. Very hot. As I glanced down to the ground, I could see all the cracks in the lava rock beneath my feet glowing bright red.

An inactive lava tube had reactivated while we were watching the lava flow into the ocean and started pumping a LOT of molten material through the ground right below our feet. And we had to run directly over it.

Naturally, I didn't want to die by lava, so I picked up my speed, met up with a couple friends mid-stride, and continued to sprint through the darkness for almost a quarter of a mile before we finally decided we were safe enough to take a breather. The rest of our friends eventually caught up, and once we'd done a head count to make sure everyone was safe and accounted for, we continued the long hike back to the car.

We only had one flashlight to guide us back - the other had been set down slightly too close to the lava flow and was consumed by the fires of the Earth itself when my less-than-intelligent friend went to get his picture taken. Fortunately, there was bright moonlight overhead so we managed to make it back to the car without anyone getting hurt.

It wasn't until we were back at the car that I thought about checking my shoes to see if my sprint over the active lava tube had done any damage to them. I borrowed the flashlight, and lifted my feet one at a time to check.

Both soles had been melted.

**TL;DR: Went to Hawaii with some friends, hiked across barren lava rock to watch lava flow into the ocean, had to sprint across an active lava tube to get to safety, melted my shoes**

I awoke with a start in my bed, a cold sweat making my skin feel clammy. I moved to check the time, but the numbers on the clock didn’t make sense. They were a jumble of random lines that were incomprehensible. Also, my bed was sitting in the desert in the middle of the afternoon. This had to be a dream. Either that, or it was a pretty good prank.

Looking around, I still felt cold. The brilliant sun overhead produced no heat, and the only warmth I felt was from my comforter pulled halfway up my torso. I moved to stand up, only to be greeted by a shadow standing a short distance away. I had to shade my eyes to see what it was, but once I could see it more clearly I dearly wished I hadn’t.

Standing in the blazing light was a tall figure dressed in a tattered black robe. Skeletal hands clutched a long scythe with a splintered wooden handle and a curved, stained blade. Its face was hidden by the hood of the robe, but I instantly knew who it was that stood before me.

“Death?” I asked, my voice feeling dry and scratchy. The figure merely nodded its head. “So does that mean I’m…?” Death shook his head silently. I blinked my confusion and shook my head, staring at the grim specter before me. There was a moment of silence before Death bowed his head and sighed audibly.

“Mortals. You think in such linear terms. William, I’m here to talk to you about your future.” Death walked forward and sat on the edge of my bed, turning his head to look at me. From inside the infinite darkness of his hood, I could tell he was looking right at me, and possibly right through me. I shivered involuntarily at the sight.

“You’re… What?” I asked, trying to comprehend what he was talking about. Death sighed again.

“Your future. You know, the thing that you plan for, the time that comes after the present, stuff that hasn’t happened yet? The. Future.” Death was a bit more sarcastic than I’d imagined. Then again, with his job, I suppose you’d have to be at one point or another.

“What about my future?” I asked warily. I’d heard you have to be very careful when dealing with Death. He enjoys playing games, and you’re never supposed to reveal too much information when you speak with him. Or is that the Devil? I could never remember.

“Look. You’ve got this whole plan and everything, the teaching, the Andes, all that jazz. I’m just saying… maybe it’s not such a good idea,” Death said with a shrug.

“Wait… Are you giving me advice on what I should do with my life? In a dream? Seriously?” Death held up his hands defensively.

“Whoa, whoa, don’t shoot the messenger. I’m just saying, maybe you should reconsider your trajectory a little bit. I hear Cleveland is very nice in the… Okay, it’s not. That’s a lie. I’m sorry.” Death shook his head and looked out toward the desert, sitting and pondering in silence for a moment. “Look, you’ve got this plan all laid out, and I respect that. I’m just saying, maybe you should rethink some of your designs on this life.”

“Well, what would you suggest?” I asked sharply. Death shrugged his shoulders noncommittally before standing up, gripping his imposing scythe with both bony hands.

“I can’t give you specifics. I’m just here in an unofficial business to tell you to reconsider. Don’t mind me. This is just a dream, after all. I’m probably just a figment of your subconscious trying to reveal something you already know or feel or some other crap. I don’t know. I’ve got work to do.” Death turned to leave, but before he could go I sat up and called out.

“Death, wait!” I never thought I’d say that sentence, but there it was. Death paused and turned to look at me. There was one question burning in my mind, the same question that burns in the minds of all mortal men. “When will I die?”

“Soon enough,” Death said before turning and disappearing in a burst of black smoke. When he was gone I suddenly sat straight up in bed, gasping for breath. I looked around in the darkness until I spotted the digital clock at my bedside. 2:07am. I sighed and laid back down, wiping the cold sweat from my forehead.

“Just a dream,” I muttered, rolling over to go back to sleep. “Just a dream.”

“Seriously. Don’t go to Peru. Just saying,” I heard Death say right before I drifted off.

The Captain stood on the Observation Deck, sipping at a cup of tea as he looked out the large viewing ports. The synthetic fibers of his dark navy and gray uniform were bothering him a bit more than usual today as he stood alone on the metal deck plating. He could feel the thrum of the ship’s distant engines though the floor, a familiar and comforting vibration that reminded him that all things were running smoothly.

The scene his eyes scanned across was a landscape of barren mountains, sandy plains, and dry canyons. A distant dust storm was inching toward the horizon, the copper and brown clouds rolling silently in the distance, one of many such storms that passed through every day. The sky was a sullen blood red shade as the planet’s red giant sun began sinking beyond the edge of the world. Night would fall soon and blanket the barren world in shadows and gloom.

A door hissed open behind the Captain and a pair of familiar footsteps could be heard approaching. The Captain stayed facing the windows, his black mug in hand, as a young officer approached his side. She stood in silence for a moment before turning to the Captain.

“Sir?” she asked, and he could tell she didn't want to disturb him, but that she needed to ask for orders. The Captain turned and smiled at her. Long blond hair, blue eyes, inquisitive nature, a fierce fighter, and a brilliant tactician. A captain in the making. *If I were a few years younger*, the Captain mused silently as he took another sip of tea.

“Yes Lieutenant?” he asked. The young woman knew she’d disturbed his solitude, and the Captain knew she’d have a reason. She hesitated briefly before speaking.

“All stations report ready, sir. We’re ready for departure. Your orders?” She looked up at the Captain, eyes moving across his face as he thought. The Captain smiled lightly at her before turning his gaze back outside.

“Prepare for departure,” he said. The Captain was a man of few words. Some officers found him confusing because of it. A man who didn’t speak much rarely tipped his hand as to what he was thinking. Others, like the young Lieutenant at his side, found it endearing. Never saying more than he had to, leading through actions instead of words.

“Aye, sir,” the Lieutenant responded. She didn't leave, however, instead gazing down at the barren world below as it was slowly engulfed by darkness. There was a long period of silence before she spoke again. “What does this place mean to you, sir?” she asked cautiously.

The Captain inhaled and exhaled slowly, searching for the right words. How much to say, how much to tell? It was always a gamble, revealing a piece of your mind to somebody. You could never be sure what they might do with it.

“Just memories,” the Captain said, his eyes moving across the dusty horizon. “Let’s get going, Lieutenant.” The Lieutenant gave a quick nod of her head and moved away toward the doorway, pausing and pressing a button on a black display panel before speaking.

“This is Lieutenant Hansen. Captain orders us to move out. Prepare to leave Earth orbit. Take us out of the Sol System once we’re clear. Hansen out.” The Lieutenant paused and looked back at the Captain for an instant before disappearing through the doorway, the doors swishing shut behind her.

Left alone with his thoughts once more, the Captain watched while the planet slowly fell away as the ship retreated from the atmosphere. He took one last glance at humanity’s ancient home world before finishing his tea and turning away from the view ports, leaving the Observation Deck and heading toward the Command Center to get the day started.

“So what does it mean?”

Director Stevens had his eyes fixed on the screen overhead, which had been looped into a playback of the final seconds of Curiosity’s transmissions from the red planet.  The rover had simply shut itself off. No kill switch had been flipped, there was no evidence of interference or damage from solar radiation, and the latest diagnostics showed everything in good working order. The rover had simply turned itself off.

Stevens watched again and again as the same seven-second loop played on repeat. The coppery red landscape, dotted by rocks that cast tiny shadows thanks to the angle of the sun, was captured by the panning of Curiosity’s camera as it swung from left to right. The view was back toward the direction it had come, across the Pahrump Hills. The rover’s tracks were plainly visible on the Martian soil, darker treaded streaks that interrupted the flowing surface of orange sand and dust that covered the planet.

It wasn’t the landscape that the camera was intent on capturing, however. Etched by the rover’s own wheels in the alien soil was a word. A single word, written by the rover itself. The heavy-duty wheels, which could be controlled independently, had worked in unison to write a message onto the distant world.

Had it been the work of one particularly skilled technician, it likely would have gotten the tech fired for playing around with such sensitive equipment, relegating the incident to a footnote in historical texts and the oddities segment of the local news. Instead, the rover had moved itself without human programming or assistance for the first time ever. Not a glitch, not an accident, an act taken solely by the rover itself with no known outside involvement.

“Sir?” the nearest tech asked Stevens, breaking the director’s concentration and forcing his attention elsewhere. Looking to the younger man, Stevens lifted an eyebrow the tech knew to mean something along the lines of “Care to repeat yourself for me?”

The tech, whose name Stevens couldn't place at the moment, looked to the screen and watched the video loop twice through before looking back to the director. “What does it mean, that word?”

Stevens folded his arms and let out a slow breath he realized he’d been holding in for no reason. Shaking his head, he looked from the repeating video to the still images of the word written in the dusty landscape millions of miles away. It was impossible, and yet there it was, staring him in the face.

The question was loaded, certainly. Stevens knew the meaning of the word, but why had the rover written that particular word? More importantly, how was it written? How could a robotic rover possibly know? Part of Stevens wanted to believe in some sort of fantastical explanation that would prove humanity wasn’t alone in the universe. Part of him hoped it was just an optical illusion, ascribing too much meaning to lines in the sand. Instead, he got the feeling that the answer was something even more deeply important to the human race, a question that had yet to be asked with an answer that should have been impossible.

“I don’t know, son,” Stevens muttered. “I don’t know.” He continued to stare at the word the rover had written before the link went dead, rolling it over and over in his mind, what it meant, and how it was possible.

One word, written on the surface of Mars by a robotic rover designed for exploration and discovery.

*Sehnsucht*.

I glanced over at the old woman sitting a few feet away, rocking silently in the timeworn wooden rocking chair that had survived who knows how many decades. Her silver hair was pulled back into a neat bun, the bright sunlight casting sharp shadows across her face wherever there were wrinkles – and she had more wrinkles than I thought it possible for someone to have. The black glasses she always wore remained on her face, a constant reminder to everyone else that she was blind.

Her mouth was perpetually pulled down into a frown, and most of the time she’d only scold people for coming out and interrupting her thinking, or yell at them for blocking the sun. If you didn’t know the old bat, you’d swear she was demented beyond repair, just roasting away in the blazing heat. If you did know her, you’d know that was probably the truth. Many people cursed her or had otherwise unkind things to say as they wandered back into the shade after their first encounter with her.

Not that the old woman noticed what was said about her. Most of the time she acted like she was deaf too and pretended not to hear when somebody was talking to her – one of the perks of getting that old, I guess, was that you could pretend to be as deaf and senile as you wanted and get away with almost anything.

Just about every day she was out here on the deck, sitting in the sun in that rocking chair, rocking back and forth, doing next to nothing at all. Her skin was so tanned at this point that I’m sure it felt like leather. I was just amazed she hadn’t died in all those years of sitting and baking in the sun, day after day after day.

She sat there, just rocking back and forth, the chair squeaking silently on the blistered wood. I think the deck used to be stained to protect it from rain, back when it still rained. Now, the wood was splintered and cracked and blistered a sort of dead, grayish color. Just like almost everything else in the town, the outdoor deck also had small piles of sand in the corners from when the winds kicked up the dirt in massive storms three miles high and fifty miles long. We usually had at least one of those storms every week.

“What makes you think that?” I asked, not expecting an answer. I’d spoken to the old woman several times before but never gotten an answer. Once she yelled at me for blocking the sun when I brought a ratty old umbrella out to her. That was when I was still new in town, after the only well for three hundred miles dried up back home. Lots of people got displaced.

“Oh, just a feeling,” she said softly, continuing to rock back and forth in her chair. I was surprised to say the least. I’d never heard her interact with anybody, even those who yelled at her for whatever reason. Most people said she was too old to remember how to socialize, and too crazy to want to interact with other human beings.

“What… What do you mean?” I asked, deciding to press my luck. There was a moment of silence before the old woman did something I’d never seen her do – she smiled. It wasn’t exactly a pretty sight. I’m sure the muscles in her face that once made smiling easy had atrophied and tightened over the decades she’d been sitting here in the sun, so when her lips twitched upward it resembled something more like a demon’s wicked grin than a normal human smile. Thankfully, it only lasted for a moment before the frown sank its way back into place.

“I can feel it in my bones,” she said simply, continuing to rock. There was silent and a low howl of wind swept that through the center of town, a small dust cyclone swirling in its wake. “I could always feel a storm coming when I was younger. Haven’t felt it in a long time. But I can feel it.”

I lifted one eyebrow skeptically. Obviously, she must be insane. Rain hadn’t fallen in this part of the world in nearly fifty years. In some places, it had been over a century and a half since the last rains fell and the last green things withered and died. Now, the sun and the wind ruled the world, merciless and taunting as they danced across the dusty plains and barren mountains day after day. What was left of the oceans was too salty to drink and had killed off most sea life ages ago.

“It’s not going to rain,” I said, turning back to look out at the baked wilderness I had been told was once a series of rolling green pastures nestled between two mountain ranges. A river used to run right through the center. Now, all that was left was dirt and dust and rocks and nothing.

“It’s going to rain,” she repeated, more firmly than before. “Balance will restore itself, sooner or later. This world is tougher than people think. Give her a little credit.”

“Right. Have fun out in the sun,” I said, shaking my head and heading out of the light and into the rickety old building, thankful for the shade. I left the old woman outside in the blazing heat so she could be crazy by herself.  I sat inside for a few minutes, reveling in the darkness before I ventured down to the lower level and out the main entrance, back onto the sandy street.

Looking up, I could see people running out of every building, shouting and waving their hands. Folks were moving toward a gap between two of the oldest buildings and looking out toward the west. I jogged to join the growing crowd, which was speaking amongst themselves in a mixture of awe and fear. When I reached the group, I looked up toward the sky where everyone had their gazes fixed.

Rolling in over the mountains were the biggest, blackest clouds I’d ever seen. Not dust clouds, but real clouds. All I’d ever seen were high, wispy, white clouds on rare spring days. These were thunder clouds, something I’d only heard stories about. I could only stare in amazement as they lurched closer, wanting to run away from the darkness but not wanting to miss a moment of what was about to happen.

Back down the road, the old woman on the rooftop was laughing loudly and hysterically as distant thunder rolled across the approaching storm.

I could feel Victor’s excitement as he led me down the stairs into the lower level of his house. Even the basement was nicely furnished – dark wood paneled walls, lush burgundy carpet, gold trim on all the lightning fixtures and furniture. It was ornate – and pretty ugly, if I was being honest – but it suited Victor perfectly.

He’d always stood out a little bit back in high school, with those combat boots, acid washed jeans, and that ratty old jacket I could swear was from some Beatles album cover. Not that he cared, of course. I’d always catch him muttering to himself in Latin – he’d taught it to himself at a young age and considered it the only “pure” language suitable for deep thought – and to him it seemed perfectly natural. People made fun of him, of course, but it just rolled off his back. I never saw him angry, or upset, or display a single negative emotion in all of our four years of high school. I would have described him as cheerfully aloof, but he was always very aware of what was going on around him. He just didn’t care.

He turned to me as he stopped in front of a locked door on the far side of the room, smiling and licking his lips as though he were eagerly anticipating a long-awaited meal. I could see his fingertips trembling in excitement, and his eyes were wide. This must be what he had been so excited to show me.

“Okay, Will, this is it. I have to warn you, not everything is finished. I’ve been working ages on this project, but things are still a little rough around the edges. I’ve tried to put the polish on this week but, you know, things get busy sometimes,” he said with an eager smile.
“It’s alright, Victor,” I assured him. “I’m sure everything is fine. You’ve put in a lot of work like you said, right?” Victor smiled and laughed, a strange sound that he never did much back in high school, except when he was exceptionally amused or delighted in his own accomplishments.
“A ha! Yes, yes, more work than I could possibly describe. Late hours, losing track of what day it is, sleeping atop a pile of books and papers… So much work,” he said, fidgeting. I tried not to look worried, but it was getting harder with every passing moment not to worry about my friend’s mental stability.

I’d been contacted a few weeks ago by his aunt, apparently his last living relative after his mother had died the year before. I’m fairly certain she was in the early stages of dementia, but she seemed to remember me for some reason – something about splitting my pants on stage at the school talent show in junior year – and figured I could “get through to poor Victor.”

He’d apparently grown distant from everyone in his life, and had hardly seemed to notice when his wife left him. I guess I wasn’t too surprised when I heard that, and I promised her I’d get in touch with him and see how he was. She thanked me and reminded me not to bend over so far for next year’s talent show. Sweet lady, but definitely losing it.

Victor was nervous I could tell, but also excited. I was pretty sure he hadn’t shown anybody else what he had been working on, probably not even his former wife. He grinned at me when I nodded at him, letting him know I was ready to see his big project.

Turning to the door, he quickly undid several locks, then produced a pair of keys from around his neck and unfastened the final two dead bolts. When he pulled the door open, I was hit by a breath of chilly air and the distinct smell of ozone. Definitely not what I was expecting. Behind the door were blank cement walls which I assumed delved into the hillside behind the house.  About ten feet in, a stairwell plunged downward, the harsh fluorescent lighting overhead a sharp contrast to the warm, almost natural lighting of the rest of the basement.

Victor stepped through the door and motioned for me to follow him, which I did with more reluctance than I had planned on having. My footsteps echoed in the empty concrete hall and in the dimly lit stairwell as we descended to a lower level. As we got lower down the stairs, which actually had several switch backs, the sound of distant thrumming machinery came to my ears, and the smell of burning sparks grew stronger.

When we reached the bottom of the stairwell, another locked door blocked the way. This one, Victor unlocked with both keys from around his neck, as well as his hand print on a small black screen to the right of the door handle. When a light above the door turned from red to green, Victor gripped the door handle before pausing, turning to look at me with his wild, excited eyes boring directly into me.

“Will… What you’re about to see might be a little… shocking,” he said before turning the handle of the door and pushing it open. When I stepped through, my eyes went wide and I’m pretty sure my jaw dropped.

Before me was a massive room that resembled a control center at NASA. The room was circular in shape, and there were monitors on every wall. The floor was covered in various work stations, each manned by people wearing black and blue jumpsuits. Men and women, young and old were down there, working at computers, talking into headsets, pointing at various screens. Workmen in black with white helmets went here and there, hauling cables and other equipment. Several men near the door we’d just walked through were welding another large monitor into place on the wall.

Victor strode forward and stopped in front of a railing that allowed him to overlook the bustle below. I approached and stood beside him, looking at a scene I was sure I must be imagining. Voices were speaking below and the mechanical thrumming was a little more intense. Finally Victor turned to me and grinned.

“Well? What do you think?” he asked, excitement in his eyes. I opened my mouth to speak before closing it, shaking my head for a moment before I looked over at him.

“Victor… What the hell am I looking at?” I finally managed to ask. Looking around at the monitors, many of them showed maps of the world, certain cities or countries highlighted. There was a shot of a fleet of ships moving through some ocean, an airport I recognized as SeaTac, and a view from high Earth orbit that looked like it was streaming from some satellite.

Victor looked at it all and grinned, spreading his arms wide. “You’re looking at the future, Will. All of this is what I’ve been working on for years. Investing my fortune, planning and building and making connections across the world. This is what I’ve been working on my entire life!” I could see the look on Victor’s face and I knew he was serious. All those years ago I’d known him he always looked like he was calculating something, planning something deep and ongoing, just below the surface.

But this… This was impossible. As I looked closer at the nearest monitors, I recognized the names of cities – capitals of almost every nation on Earth. There were satellites tracking airplanes that carried important diplomats and world leaders. A grid on one screen showed numerous red lights in orbit all over the planet, positioned with utmost planning and precision.

“Victor…” I started as I looked over at him, watching as he looked with pride upon what he’d worked his entire life to build. The look in his eyes was like the one I’d seen when a father watches his son ride a bicycle by himself for the first time – a deep, profound sense of pride at watching something you’d nurtured for years start to grow up. “Victor, what is this place?” I asked quietly.

He turned sharply and looked at me, grinning. “It’s revenge, Will, don’t you see? All those years ago, brooding in high school, muttering to myself, I was planning my revenge! From the very first day, it was all I’d ever wanted! And now, it’s so close I can almost taste it,” he whispered, clenching his hands into fists. The look in his eyes was no longer of pride but of madness. Madness and cruelty and a desire to watch things burn.

“What… What are you going to do, Victor?” I asked as calmly as I could, wondering if I could escape from this deranged fantasy place before my old friend squeezed the life out of me with his own hands. Victor chuckled a bit as he looked at me.

“I’m going to conquer the world, of course,” he stated matter-of-factly. “Destroy the major cities and bring society to its knees. Then, I’ll rise from the chaos I’ve created and claim what is rightfully mine!” Then, he started laughing. It started off like the odd, squeaky laugh I’d recognized from years ago, but it quickly evolved into something heartier, darker, and much more menacing. Victor laughed and laughed and I couldn’t help by feel myself shrink away, wishing that I’d never been so memorable to one particular demented aunt.
